excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: By the heaven some understand the supreme heaven, the heaven of heavens, the habitation of God, and of the holy angels; and this being made perfect at once, no mention is after made of it, as of the earth … but rather the lower and visible heavens are meant, at least are not excluded, that is, the substance of them…
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly dissolves the Gen 1:1 vs 1:8 tension by distinguishing two heavens: the 'heaven of heavens' made at once in v.1, and the lower visible heavens whose firmament is later named Heaven in v.8.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Nor does it appear that the atmosphere is particularly intended here, as this is spoken of, Gen 1:6, under the term firmament. The word heavens must therefore comprehend the whole solar system, as it is very likely the whole of this was created in these six days…
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes the 'heavens' of Gen 1:1 (the whole solar system) from the firmament named Heaven in Gen 1:6-8, so the two passages refer to different things rather than contradicting on timing.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The happiness of heaven, though prepared before the foundation of the world, yet must be further fitted up for man in his fallen state.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reconciles the New Testament side of the tension: heaven is 'prepared from the foundation of the world' (Matt 25:34) yet Jesus still 'goes to prepare a place' (John 14:2), by reading the latter as a further fitting-up of an already-created glory.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: This must refer to some intelligent beings who existed before the creation of the visible heavens and earth: and it is supposed that this and the following clause refer to the same beings; that by the sons of God, and the morning stars, the angelic host is meant… Perhaps their creation may be included in the term heavens, Gen 1:1: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.”
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the chronology: the 'morning stars' of Job 38:7 are not the literal stars made on day four but the angelic host created with the 'heavens' of Gen 1:1, so there is no conflict.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: when the morning-stars sang together, the blessed angels (the first-born of the Father of light), who, in the morning of time, shone as brightly as the morning star, going immediately before the light which God commanded to shine out of darkness upon the seeds of this lower world, the earth, which was without form and void.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reads the 'morning stars' as the angels present at the founding of the earth, dissolving the apparent priority of stars over the earth in Job 38:7.

excerpts.author: Tyndale
excerpts.attribution: Tyndale Open Bible Commentary
excerpts.excerpt_text: The morning stars are personified in parallel construction with the angels (1:6; 2:1).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A modern, concise version of the same harmonization: the morning stars are a poetic parallel to the angels, not the literal stars of Genesis 1, so the day-four ordering stands.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Many have asked, “How could light be produced on the first day, and the sun, the fountain of it, not created till the fourth day?”… I therefore conclude, that as God has diffused the matter of caloric or latent heat through every part of nature, without which there could be neither vegetation nor animal life, that it is caloric or latent heat which is principally intended by the original word.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the contradiction outright and resolves it by distinguishing the day-one 'light' (a diffused light/heat) from the sun later constituted on day four, so light and its division can precede the luminaries.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: the body of fire and light produced on the first day was now distributed and formed into several luminous bodies of sun, moon, and stars, for these were “from light”; lights produced from that light, or made out of it… as the light by its circular motion did for the first three days, or the diurnal motion of the earth on its axis, then and now…
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Harmonizes the two divisions by making the day-four luminaries a redistribution of the day-one light, so the same light that divided day from night on day one is concentrated into the sun and moon on day four.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Both these lights may be said to be “made” on the fourth day—not created, indeed, for it is a different word that is here used, but constituted, appointed to the important and necessary office of serving as luminaries to the world, and regulating by their motions and their influence the progress and divisions of time.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes creating from constituting: the luminaries were not first created on day four but appointed to their light-dividing office, so the day-one division of light from darkness is not duplicated or contradicted.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: And these are the sons of Dishon,…. Not of Dishon the son of Anah, but of Dishon the son of Seir
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the tension by distinguishing two men named Dishon — son of Seir versus son of Anah — which dissolves the grandfather/father conflict.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: neither will he keep his anger for ever; though he does with the wicked, yet not with his own people; that endures but for a moment, and is rather seeming than real
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the moment-vs-forever conflict by distinguishing God's enduring anger toward the wicked from His momentary anger toward His own people.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Though God may for a time lay his own people under the tokens of his displeasure, yet he will not retain his anger for ever, but though he cause grief he will have compassion; he is not implacable; yet against those that are not of the remnant of his heritage, that are unpardoned, he will keep his anger for ever.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States both poles explicitly and harmonizes them: anger is not retained for ever toward His own people, yet is kept for ever against the unpardoned.

excerpts.author: Keil & Delitzsch
excerpts.work: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament
excerpts.attribution: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the OT (1861-75)
excerpts.excerpt_text: wrath is, in relation to them, only a vanishing moment: a moment passes in His anger, a (whole) life in His favour, i.e., the former endures only for a moment, the latter the whole life of a man.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Frames the duration of divine anger as momentary relative to the pious, set against a whole life of favour, harmonizing the brevity texts with the long-anger texts via the qualifier 'in relation to them'.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: There it was said that the centurion came to Christ; here it is said that he sent to him first some of the elders of the Jews (Luk 7:3), and afterwards some other friends, Luk 7:6. But it is a rule that we are said to do that which we do by another - Quod facimus per alium, id ipsum facere judicamur. The centurion might be said to do that which he did by his proxies; as a man takes possession by his attorney. But it is probable that the centurion himself came at last
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the exact difference (came vs. sent elders/friends) and resolves it by the legal-agency maxim that one is said to do what one does through proxies, adding that the centurion probably came in person at the end.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: In the parallel place in Matthew, he is represented as coming to Christ himself; but it is a usual form of speech in all nations, to attribute the act to a person which is done not by himself, but by his authority.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gives the same agency harmonization concisely: Matthew's 'he came' is the ordinary idiom of crediting to a person what is done in his name by his deputies.

excerpts.author: Tyndale
excerpts.attribution: Tyndale Open Bible Commentary
excerpts.excerpt_text: With his tendency to abbreviate accounts, Matthew has the centurion approaching Jesus (Matt 8:5-13). Luke tells the full story in which Jewish elders, and later the centurion’s friends, act as intermediaries.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A distinct modern voice resolving the tension by compositional abbreviation: Matthew compresses the account so the centurion 'approaches' directly, while Luke preserves the intermediaries.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: It is now generally thought by the best critics that, through an error of the copyists, an omission has been made of the oldest son's name, and that Vashni, which is not the name of a person, merely signifies “and the second.” This critical emendation of the text makes all clear, as well as consistent with other passages relating to the family of Samuel.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the Joel/Vashni conflict by treating 'Vashni' as not a name at all but a corruption of the Hebrew for 'and the second,' with the firstborn Joel's name dropped by a copyist.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The word יואל Joel is lost out of the text in this place, and ושני vesheni, which signifies the second, and which refers to Abiah, is made here into a proper name. The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Chaldee, copy this blunder; but the Syriac and Arabic read as in Sa1 8:2.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gives the same copyist-error harmonization with the Hebrew and the versional evidence: Joel dropped out, 'vesheni' ('the second') mistaken for a name, and the Syriac and Arabic still agreeing with 1 Samuel 8:2.

excerpts.author: Keil & Delitzsch
excerpts.work: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament
excerpts.attribution: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the OT (1861-75)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The sons are also mentioned again in Ch1 6:13, though the name of the elder has either been dropped out of the Masoretic text or has become corrupt.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A distinct critical voice giving the same resolution from the 1 Samuel side: the elder son's name in the Chronicles parallel was either dropped from the Masoretic text or corrupted.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The royal progress was of public importance. It was a season of national devotion. The king was accompanied by his principal nobility (Ch2 1:2)
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the tension: reads the bare Kings notice as the same public, nobility-attended event Chronicles describes, so the congregation's presence is assumed rather than absent.

excerpts.author: Keil & Delitzsch
excerpts.work: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament
excerpts.attribution: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the OT (1861-75)
excerpts.excerpt_text: While in Kg1 3:4 it is briefly said the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, our historian records that Solomon summoned the princes and representatives of the people to this solemn act, and accompanied by them went to Gibeon. This sacrifice was no mere private sacrifice-it was the religious consecration of the opening of his reign, at which the estates of the kingdom were present as a matter of course.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the exact contrast (Kings brief vs. Chronicles' summoned assembly) and treats the two as independent accounts of one event, with the congregation present as a matter of course.

excerpts.author: Tyndale
excerpts.attribution: Tyndale Open Bible Commentary
excerpts.excerpt_text: Solomon’s journey to Gibeon, reported in 1 Kgs 3:4, is here elaborated. This great public venture was closely associated with Solomon taking the throne. The event included military commanders and clan leaders.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly frames Chronicles as an elaboration of the same 1 Kings 3:4 journey, supplying the public, attended character the Kings text leaves unstated.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The very brief reign of this prince, which lasted only three months, during which he was a humble vassal of the Assyrians, is scarcely deserving to be taken into account, and therefore is in no way contradictory to the prophetic menace denounced against his father (Jer 36:30).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the contradiction explicitly and resolves it: Jehoiachin's three-month reign is too slight to count, so it does not falsify Jeremiah's word that Jehoiakim would have none on the throne.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: As this man reigned only three months and was a mere vassal to the Babylonians, his reign is scarcely to be reckoned; and therefore Jeremiah says of Jehoiakim, He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David, Jer 36:30, for at that time it belonged to the king of Babylon, and Jehoiachin was a mere viceroy or governor.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Same harmonizing reckoning from a distinct voice: a three-month vassal reign is not truly a reign, so Jeremiah's saying stands without conflict.

excerpts.author: Keil & Delitzsch
excerpts.work: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament
excerpts.attribution: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the OT (1861-75)
excerpts.excerpt_text: And even though his son Jehoiachin ascended the throne after his father's death and maintained his position for three months against the Chaldaeans, until at length he fell into their hands and was carried away alive to Babylon, the prophet might very truly describe this short reign as not sitting upon the throne of David (cf. Graf on Jer 22:19).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A third, critical-grammatical voice grounding the same reading: a three-month reign ending in deportation does not amount to 'sitting upon the throne of David,' reconciling 2 Kings with Jeremiah.

excerpts.author: Tyndale
excerpts.attribution: Tyndale Open Bible Commentary
excerpts.excerpt_text: The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish (1:6; 34:15-16).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The cleanest temporary-vs-final harmonization: the wicked prosper 'for a time' (Job/Ps 73/Jer) yet 'ultimately perish' (Ps 34:21), so both poles describe different stages of one outcome.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: This principle Job here opposes, and maintains that God, in disposing men’s outward affairs, acts as a sovereign, reserving the exact distribution of rewards and punishments for the future state.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Concedes the wicked do prosper now (Job 12:6) but locates the corrective justice (Ps 34:21) in the future state, dissolving the conflict by separating present lot from final reckoning.

excerpts.author: Geneva Bible (annotators)
excerpts.attribution: Geneva Bible (1599)
excerpts.excerpt_text: God for a while giveth prosperity, that afterward they should the more feel his heavy judgment when they lack their riches which were a sign of his mercy.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A distinct 1599 voice making the same temporary-vs-final move: present prosperity ('for a while') is itself a setup for the heavier judgment to come, so Jer 12:1 and Ps 34:21 are stages of one process.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: This restraint was upon them only in their first mission, afterwards they were appointed to go into all the world, and teach all nations.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes the two poles by making the restriction temporary (the first mission) and the universal commission its later supersession.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Until Christ’s death, which broke down the middle wall of Partition (Eph 2:14), the Gospel commission was to the Jews only
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gives the classic temporal harmonization: the Jews-only restriction held only until Christ's death removed the Jew/Gentile partition, after which the mission opens.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: before it was confined to Judea, but now it is extended to all the nations of the world; see Mat 10:6
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Voices the harmonization from the commission side, expressly cross-referencing the earlier restriction (Mat 10:6) as the prior, now-superseded stage.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The other evangelists, Matthew and Mark, say it was six days after: the reason of this difference is, because Luke takes in the day in which he delivered these sayings, and that in which he was transfigured, and they only reckon the intermediate days
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the six-vs-eight-days conflict as inclusive vs. exclusive counting: Luke counts the day of the saying and the day of the event, Matthew and Mark count only the days between.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: an eight days after these sayings--including the day on which this was spoken and that of the Transfiguration. Matthew and Mark say (Mat 17:1; Mar 9:2) “after six days,” excluding these two days.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States the same harmonization in mirror form from the Luke side: Luke's eight days include the two endpoint days that Matthew and Mark exclude.

excerpts.author: Geneva Bible (annotators)
excerpts.attribution: Geneva Bible (1599)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Luke reckoneth eight days, containing in that number the first and last, and Matthew speaketh but of them that were betwixt them.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A distinct, terse sixteenth-century voice giving the identical reckoning: Luke counts the first and last day, Matthew only the days in between.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Having seized him, they led him away to Annas first, before they brought him to the court that was sat, expecting him, in the house of Caiaphas… Annas did not long detain them, being as willing as any of them to have the prosecution pushed on, and therefore sent him bound to Caiaphas, to his house, which was appointed for the rendezvous of the sanhedrim upon this occasion
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes the sequence: the visit to Annas was a short preliminary stop before the prisoner was sent on to Caiaphas's house, where the sanhedrin (the Synoptics' trial) was already convened.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: It is likely that Annas was chief of the Sanhedrin, and that it was to him in that office that Christ was first brought… What is related in the 24th verse, Now Annas had sent him bound to Caiaphas, comes properly in after the 13th verse.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Resolves the order by Annas's standing (head of the council) and by reading John 18:24 as belonging right after 18:13, so the Annas stage is momentary before the transfer to Caiaphas the Synoptics report.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: therefore they first lead him to him, to have his advice how to proceed, and to take him along with them to his son-in-law, where the great council was convened, and that he might use his interest and authority, in taking proper measures, in order to put Jesus to death
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A distinct voice giving a motive for the extra Annas stage: it was a consultative call before proceeding to Caiaphas's house, where the council was already assembled, so John's order and the Synoptics' destination coincide.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: He bore it all alone first; when he could no longer carry the whole through weakness, occasioned by the ill usage he had received, Simon, a Cyrenian, helped him to carry it
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The most direct harmonization: Jesus carried the cross alone at first (John), and Simon was compelled only when weakness made him unable to continue (the Synoptics) — one sequence, not two accounts in conflict.

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.attribution: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary (1871)
excerpts.excerpt_text: It would appear that our Lord had first to bear His own cross (Joh 19:17), but being from exhaustion unable to proceed, it was laid on another to bear it “after Him.”
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A distinct voice that names John 19:17 explicitly against Luke and resolves the tension by sequence — Jesus first, Simon taking it over from exhaustion.

excerpts.author: Geneva Bible (annotators)
excerpts.attribution: Geneva Bible (1599)
excerpts.excerpt_text: They compelled Simon to bear his burdensome cross, whereby it appeareth that Jesus was so sore handled before, that he fainted by the way, and was not able to bear his cross throughout: for John writeth that he did bear the cross, to wit, at the beginning.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A third distinct voice harmonizing the Synoptics with John on the same sequential ground — John has Jesus bearing it at the beginning; Simon was compelled because Jesus could not bear it throughout.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The Evangelist John calls it a “title”, Joh 19:19, and Luke, a “superscription”, Luk 23:38, and Mark, the “superscription of his accusation”, Mar 15:26, it was what contained the sum and substance of what he was accused, and for which he was condemned, and suffered.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill harmonizes the four evangelists' differing labels for the placard by treating them as one inscription holding the same 'sum and substance' of the accusation, dissolving the wording difference.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Matthew called it, aitia - the accusation; Mark and Luke called it epigraphē - the inscription; John calls it by the proper Latin name, titlos - the title: and it was this, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry lines up the evangelists' varying terms for the same placard and gives the fullest Johannine form, treating the divergent reports as one title rather than conflicting wordings.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: John only mentions Mary of Magdala, because he appears to wish to give a more detailed history of her conduct than of any of the rest; but the other evangelists speak of three persons who went together to the tomb, viz. Mary of Magdala, Mary the mother of James, and Salome: Mat 28:1; Mar 16:1.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the count tension: John names only Mary Magdalene because his interest is in her, while the other evangelists report multiple women — selective focus, not conflicting numbers.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: This evangelist does not mention the other women that went with Mary Magdalene, but here only, because she was the most active and forward in this visit to the sepulchre, and in her appeared the most affection
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A second, distinct voice harmonizing John's single name with the others' larger groups on the same ground — John records only Mary Magdalene because she was foremost, not because she came alone.

excerpts.author: Adam Clarke
excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: This vinegar must not be confounded with the vinegar and gall mentioned Mat 27:34, and Mar 15:23. That, being a stupifying potion, intended to alleviate his pain, he refused to drink; but of this he took a little, and then expired, Joh 19:30.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke explicitly separates the two drinks: the stupefying potion of the Synoptics was refused, while the plain vinegar of John was received, dissolving the refuse-versus-drink tension by distinguishing the offers.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: They had given him vinegar to drink before they crucified him (Mat 27:34), but the prophecy was not exactly fulfilled in that, because that was not in his thirst; therefore now he said, I thirst, and called for it again: then he would not drink, but now he received it
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry assigns the refusal and the reception to two distinct moments ('then he would not drink, but now he received it'), directly reconciling the Synoptic refusal with the Johannine drinking.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: indeed Mark says, they gave him “wine mingled with myrrh”, Mar 15:23; which was either a cordial provided by his friends, and given him, and is different from what the soldiers gave him here … he thought fit to taste of it in a superficial way, to show he did not despise nor resent their offer; and that he was really athirst, and ready to drink a more disagreeable potion than that,
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill distinguishes Mark's myrrh-wine from the soldiers' vinegar-and-gall and reads the Synoptic 'tasting' as a deliberate, superficial gesture rather than a flat refusal, harmonizing the accounts of whether He drank.
